---
title: "Vision Transformer (ViT)"
description: "A vision model that processes image patches as tokens using Transformer layers."
term: "Vision Transformer (ViT)"
letter: "V"
category: "Computer Vision"
difficulty: "Intermediate"
---

## Simple explanation

A Vision Transformer splits an image into small patches, turns each patch into
a vector, and processes the resulting sequence with Transformer layers.

## Technical explanation

For an image of dimensions $H\times W$ and patch size $P$, non-overlapping
patches are projected to embeddings, typically producing
$N=(H/P)(W/P)$ tokens. Positional information is added before self-attention
layers combine information across patches. Classification models often use a
special class token or pool patch features.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

ViTs provide a flexible architecture for image classification and broader
vision tasks, and can scale effectively with large training data. They may
require substantial data or pretraining to match convolutional inductive
biases, and high-resolution inputs increase token count and attention cost.

## How it works

Patchify the image, project each flattened patch, add positional embeddings,
and pass the sequence through Transformer blocks. A task-specific head maps
the resulting representation to predictions.

## Practical example

For image classification, resize training and inference images consistently,
split them into patches, and fine-tune a pretrained ViT. Compare quality and
latency against a convolutional baseline at the same image resolution.

## Common misconceptions

- A ViT does not process an image as a single undifferentiated vector; it
  retains a sequence of patch tokens and positional information.
- Transformers are not automatically superior to convolutional models for
  every image size, dataset, or deployment budget.
